source_read: PMC full text PMC10231478, read in the app's browser in a tab of my own (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10231478/): every section, Tables 1-4 with their footnotes (rendered as text), the figure captions, and the contributor, funding, competing-interest, ethics and data statements. Figures 1 (flowchart) and 2 (Kaplan-Meier curves) are images; their values were not extracted beyond the text. The article has no supplement. The Table 3 'p for trend' value (0.038) sits in the fifth cell of its row, the IR column, checked in the page's table cells after the browser bridge came back (second visit, new tab).

key_findings.note: Methods > Study population 1st paragraph (aged 18 or older, first arrest = index date, every arrest with a positive urine test, encrypted-ID linkage, comparisons insured in the index year, four per exposed person frequency matched on index year, age and sex; prior psychosis excluded for comparisons), 2nd paragraph (prior psychosis excluded for all subjects; final 74,601 and 298,404) and Findings 1st paragraph.

I counted 23 names in the Study population 1st paragraph, including methamphetamine, its racemate and levomethamphetamine, amphetamine, dexamphetamine, levamphetamine, MDMA, MDA, MDEA, brolamfetamine, DOM (4-methyl-2,5-dimethoxyamphetamine) and lisdexamphetamine. No breakdown by substance appears anywhere in the text or tables.
Findings 1st paragraph and Table 1 (counts reproduce the percentages, e.g. 1,476/74,601 = 1.98%); the 2007-2016 window for comorbidities is in Study population 3rd paragraph.

Table 2 All row and Findings 2nd paragraph. Recomputed: 1,722/367,696 = 4.68 and 1,144/1,487,536 = 0.77 per 1,000; rate difference 3.91 per 1,000 person-years; the crude HR 6.08 equals the rate ratio 4.68/0.77.
Findings 2nd paragraph ('six-fold higher', 3.75% vs 0.63%, log-rank p<0.0001).

All values match Table 2. The Findings 3rd paragraph covers only the age strata (largest HR at 45 or older); the sex results are in Table 2 (and the abstract and Conclusions 1st and 4th paragraphs). No interaction test anywhere.

Table 2 Comorbidities rows; Findings 3rd paragraph; Conclusions 3rd paragraph ('inferring a direct effect'). Recomputed differences: 20.02 - 7.39 = 12.63 and 3.91 - 0.62 = 3.29 per 1,000; baseline rates differ 11.9-fold.

Table 3 values all match; Findings 4th paragraph; Statistics 1st paragraph (arrests counted from the index date to the study end date); Conclusions 3rd paragraph (no validated measures of dose, frequency, amount or severity). Recomputed: person-years per person 4.37 (one arrest) to 6.48 (five or more); a linear regression of the five category rates on arrests 1-5 gives slope 0.214, t = 3.56, df 3, p = 0.0377, matching the printed 0.038. Adding the zero-arrest category gives p = 0.070 and a regression of the log adjusted HRs gives p = 0.004, so only the five-rate regression reproduces the printed value.

Table 4 and its footnote (adjusted for age, sex, number of arrests and comorbidities); Conclusions 8th paragraph (about 10%, chosen by prosecutors for promising outcomes; treatment in hospital psychiatric departments may raise the chance of a diagnosis). 7,733/74,601 = 10.4%. The 5th paragraph is where the authors call it psychotherapy.
Study population 2nd paragraph, both code lists as printed.

key_findings.correction: Replace 'arrests reflect police activity and miss most use' with 'arrests reflect police activity and priorities and do not capture all use (many people who use are never arrested)'. The authors say arrests do not capture all use and that many people who use will never be detected or arrested; 'most' is not their word. The rest of the list matches the Conclusions 6th to 10th paragraphs (precipitate rather than cause, 6th; severity not documented and socio-economic status not matched, 7th; prosecutors' selection of about 10%, no genetic data, ethnic group, obstetric complications or childhood adversity, 8th; four controls per case and a single average HR, 9th; no time-varying analysis, 10th).

key_findings.note: Conclusions 2nd paragraph. 77/31.7 = 2.43 and 77/26.6 = 2.89 recomputed. The paper prints the two rates as '77 and 468 per 100 000 persons' and calls them annual cumulative incidence rates; the card's reading of them as rates per person-year (Table 2) is correct.

reporting_issues.note: Study population 2nd paragraph: the included diagnoses name 'other stimulant use disorders with psychosis'; 292.1, 292.11 and 292.12 are in the exclusion list only.

Study population 3rd paragraph (diagnosed during 2007-2016) against the Table 1 title (baseline); 296.24 and 296.34 are in both the depression codes and the outcome codes. A further, immaterial overlap: 300.4 is a depression code and also falls inside the anxiety code 300.
Study population 3rd paragraph (18-35, 35-49, 50 or older) against Tables 1 and 2 (18-29, 30-44, 45 or older).

Recomputed as in key finding 7 (p = 0.0377 from the five category rates; 0.070 with the zero category; 0.004 from log HRs). On the last sentence: the Statistics 1st paragraph says arrests were counted from the index date 'to the study end date', which reads as counting arrests after a diagnosis too; 'probably counted, not stated explicitly' would be closer than 'not stated'.
The printed unit is 'per 100 000 persons' (Conclusions 2nd paragraph); the point stands.
Abstract Findings (5.28) and Findings 2nd paragraph (6.08), same phrase.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E fits an observational exposure cohort. I agree with every domain and with overall very high. Confounding very high rather than high: the comparison group has no record of any illicit drug use, so other drug use (cannabis included), alcohol and their correlates differ by design and none is adjusted for, while the adjustment set includes diagnoses made after the index date, two of them outcome codes. That is the 'important confounders not controlled, likely substantial' case, plus adjustment for variables partly downstream of exposure and partly the outcome itself. The crude-to-adjusted fall (6.08 to 5.28) comes partly from adjusting for a depression variable that contains outcome codes.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: High: specific for some use at the arrest, insensitive (comparison group may include people who use), fixed at the first arrest, 23 substances pooled. In addition, an arrest can follow behaviour during an untreated psychotic episode, which would make exposure partly an effect of the outcome.
High: follow-up starts at the first arrest, not at the start of use, and the look-back for earlier diagnoses is not stated.
Some concerns is reasonable (counts at each step only in the flowchart image; deaths not reported).
High: unvalidated claims codes and more contact with services after arrest, which the authors themselves note for the rehabilitation group.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. The abstract and Conclusions use causal wording for the rehabilitation contrast ('preventive effect of psychotherapy', 5th paragraph; 'appears to be mitigated through psychotherapy', 11th paragraph) and for the comorbidity strata ('direct effect', 3rd paragraph), which the design cannot support. The card's five gaps are all verified against the text.

missed: Competing risk of death (minor): the Cox models and the Kaplan-Meier curves treat death as censoring, and the number of deaths is not reported. The 10-year cumulative incidences (3.75% vs 0.63%) are therefore Kaplan-Meier estimates for a world without death; they overstate the actual cumulative incidence somewhat, more in the cohort with higher mortality. Claims citing '3.75% over 10 years' could say 'Kaplan-Meier estimate'.

Sex difference (minor): the Conclusions 4th paragraph calls the larger HR in women 'amphetamine induced psychosis' and gives a biological explanation, but the same paragraph offers a confounding explanation (women arrested were more disadvantaged: trauma, less psychosocial support, stigma). The card reports the sex HRs but does not list this causal reading among the gaps.

Small point on the card's 'unmeasured_premorbid' field: the authors name missing genetic data, ethnic group, obstetric complications and childhood adversity (Conclusions 8th paragraph); 'family history of psychosis' is the card's addition, not one the authors name. Other drug use was recorded in the same database (the comparison group is defined by having no such record) but was not used, so for other drugs 'not adjusted for' is more accurate than 'not measured'.
